turns.en: So, we've been chatting about your famous giveaway, your Legos career advice. This idea of how this advice applies in today's very strange AI world.

ts.sec: Early scaling at Google and Facebook

turns.en: It was 500 employees and 80 million users, smaller than MySpace, which is always good context to remember. And while I was there, obviously a huge growth curve. I left 5 years later; it was 5,500 employees and over a billion users. So that experience was nuts from a scaling perspective.
turns.zh: 当时是 500 名员工和 8000 万用户，比 MySpace 还小，这个背景值得记住。我在那里时，显然经历了巨大的增长曲线。5 年后我离开时，公司有 5500 名员工和超过 10 亿用户。所以从 Scaling（规模扩张）的角度看，那段经历简直疯狂。

turns.en: And what I witnessed at Google and then really witnessed at Facebook was how hard and scary that experience was for people. I watched a lot of folks go from building a thing—you show up and you become the person that owns the blog or owns this part of the stack or built that product—and you build an identity around it. You're that person, whatever that is. And then the nature of scale is that everything around you changes. Somebody shows up and your manager says, "Hey, you need to hand that thing that you've built your whole identity around to someone else and go on to doing something else." And your first instinct is like, "What? No, I don't want to give it away. I'm good at this. I know how to do this. I also think it's fun, and what if it's the only fun thing to do?" So you witness people having this tendency to hold on.
turns.zh: 我在 Google 目睹、后来在 Facebook 真正见证的是，这种经历对人们来说有多艰难、多可怕。我看到很多人从「你做出一个东西」开始——你加入，成为拥有那个博客、拥有技术栈那一部分、做出那个产品的人——并围绕它建立身份认同。你就是那个人，不管那是什么。然后 Scaling（规模扩张）的本质就是，你周围的一切都在变。有人来了，你的经理说：「嘿，你需要把你整个身份认同所系的那个东西交给别人，然后去做别的事。」你的第一反应是：「什么？不，我不想交出去。我擅长这个。我知道怎么做。而且我觉得这很有趣，万一这是唯一有趣的事呢？」所以你看到人们有这种紧抓不放的倾向。

turns.en: So what I started to do with people on my team was say, "Hey, this change is happening and here's how you might feel—you might feel territorial and want to hold on." And actually the most important thing to do is to give things away, to evolve as the company is evolving. And my brain is a really weird place. I grew up on the Muppets, so I always think there's just a lot of tiny monsters dancing around singing songs in my head. But that is why metaphors come out for me. And so I always use this metaphor of a bunch of kindergarteners and somebody dumps a pile of Legos in front of you. At first it's fun, a little overwhelming, then you start building. And the give-away-your-Legos part is like that feeling when somebody else shows up and they try to take the tower out of your hands, and the kindergartener response is like, "Get out of here." You know what I mean? It's like shoving someone away. When actually, if you get multiple people, it means oh, you can go build something new and fun. You can start from scratch and you can learn something. But the natural human instinct in the face of change is to hold on to things and to resist the change, to be territorial and all of those things.
turns.zh: 所以我开始对我团队里的人说：「嘿，这种变化正在发生，你可能会这样感觉——你可能会感到领地意识，想要紧抓不放。」而实际上最重要的事情是放手，随着公司的发展而进化。我的大脑是个很奇怪的地方。我是看《布偶秀》长大的，所以我总觉得脑子里有很多小怪物在跳舞唱歌。但这就是为什么我总能冒出比喻。我总用这个比喻：一群幼儿园小朋友，有人在你面前倒了一堆乐高。一开始很好玩，有点应接不暇，然后你开始搭建。而「交出你的乐高」这部分，就像别人出现，试图从你手里拿走那座塔时的那种感觉，幼儿园小朋友的反应是「滚开」。你懂我的意思吗？就像把别人推开。但实际上，如果你有多个人，就意味着你可以去搭建新的、好玩的东西。你可以从零开始，可以学到东西。但面对变化时，人类的本能就是紧抓不放、抗拒变化，变得有领地意识，诸如此类。

turns.en: So anyway, I started giving this talk to folks on my team to help them understand that change and what was coming. The talk I was—when I was at Facebook, it was over 20 years ago. And I sent it to First Round and we published it. And I would have said I was speaking to folks going through a Facebook-like experience. I would have said, "Hey, this is an article that is for the Stripes or the Slacks or whoever was blowing up in 2013, to normalize, hey, this is what it feels like and this is what you have to do to grow as fast as your company is growing." But what happened when it was published is that I got emails from all over the world. I got emails from people at companies like Safeway, where this woman—I still remember this email—wrote me and was like, "This was so helpful to me. This perfectly describes what I've been going through on my team." And I got an email again, I remember it very vividly, from a founder in Nigeria who was like, "My team went from two people to four people this year and give away your Legos is so valuable to me. This is exactly what I've been feeling." And my first reaction was like, I didn't write this for you. This was not meant for you. But my second one was, whoa, this is about something much bigger than just what it feels like to be inside of rapid scale.
turns.zh: 总之，我开始给我团队里的人做这个演讲，帮他们理解那种变化和即将到来的东西。后来我把它发给了 First Round 的朋友们，他们当时正在做 First Round Review。说清楚一点，这是 13 年前的事了。我在 Facebook 时，那是 20 多年前。我把它发给 First Round，我们发表了。我本来会说，我是在对经历类似 Facebook 体验的人讲话。我本来会说：「嘿，这篇文章是给 2013 年那些正在爆发的 Stripe 或 Slack 之类的公司看的，是为了让这件事正常化：这就是它的感觉，这就是你要做的，才能跟上公司增长的速度。」但文章发表后发生的是，我收到了来自世界各地的邮件。我收到了来自 Safeway 这类公司的人的邮件，有位女士——我还记得这封邮件——写信给我说：「这对我太有帮助了。它完美地描述了我一直在团队里经历的事情。」我还收到一封邮件，我记得非常清楚，来自尼日利亚的一位创始人，他说：「我的团队今年从两个人变成四个人，『交出你的乐高』对我来说太有价值了。这正是我一直以来的感受。」我的第一反应是，我不是为你写的。这不是给你看的。但我的第二个反应是，哇，这关乎的东西比身处快速 Scaling（规模扩张）中的感受要大得多。

turns.en: And fundamentally, I think the Legos message is about change. It's about the fact that when you go through change, a lot happens to you. It's a very specific experience, and I think that's why it ended up being so universal. And it is crazy—I still get emails about it, multiple emails a month about it to this day. So it's lasted in a way that, again, I just thought I was sending out a note to folks going through crazy rapid change. I was at a First Round event, I don't know, a year ago or something, and they were talking about all the different posts people have written, and I think it's one of the maybe the first or second most popular post on the First Round Review.
turns.zh: 从根本上说，我认为「乐高」这个信息是关于变化的。它关乎一个事实：当你经历变化时，很多事情会发生在你身上。这是一种非常具体的体验，我想这就是为什么它最终如此普遍适用。而且很疯狂——我至今仍收到关于它的邮件，每个月好几封。所以它以某种方式持续了下来，再说一次，我原以为我只是给经历疯狂快速变化的人发了一封便条。我在一个 First Round 活动上，大概是去年吧，他们在谈论人们写的各种文章，我想它可能是 First Round Review 上最受欢迎的第一或第二篇文章。

turns.en: It's up there and it's traveled in ways that I don't think any of us imagined it would.
turns.zh: 它确实名列前茅，而且传播的方式我想我们谁都没想象到。

turns.en: Okay, so let's talk about what still holds true in this advice in today's very strange AI world. What still holds true? What's still correct about this advice based on what you're seeing?
turns.zh: 好，那我们来谈谈在如今这个非常奇怪的 AI 世界里，这个建议中还有哪些依然成立。哪些依然成立？根据你所看到的，这个建议中还有哪些是正确的？

turns.en: One thing that's crazy about this article is I still get so many emails about it today. I still get asked to give speeches at every fast-growing company. So I think for anybody that's going through rapid scale, Legos is still really relevant. But the interesting thing is what started to happen, probably like two years ago, is I got more inbound from managers and more inbound from leaders about Legos—just more people grappling with change inside their companies. And I think that is the thing that really holds true today and actually has just become more universal.
turns.zh: 这篇文章疯狂的一点是，我今天仍然收到很多关于它的邮件。我仍然被邀请去每一家快速成长的公司演讲。所以我认为，对于任何正在经历快速 Scaling（规模扩张）的人来说，「乐高」仍然非常相关。但有趣的是，大概两年前开始发生的是，我从管理者那里收到的来信更多了，从领导者那里收到的关于「乐高」的来信也更多了——只是有更多人在公司内部应对变化。我认为这正是今天依然成立、而且实际上变得更加普遍的事情。

turns.en: I used to really check before I went and did a speech at some company how fast the company was growing. I would ask about revenue growth and about headcount growth because that just helps me contextualize how I should speak to employees, and I still do that. But it's also become really clear that every single company in the world is going through enormous change of varying shapes and kinds right now. And that is the fundamental underlying message of Legos: how do you deal with change and how do you be your best self in the face of change. So I feel like the number one thing that is true today as true as it was 10 or 15 years ago is the change is really scary and hard. And I always say—somebody once asked me to summarize the Legos article in one sentence. They're like, "Molly, this is too long, give me the cliff notes." And I said two things. Because I do think leaning on each other to learn what's real and what's not and what's valuable and what's not—so much of what we're doing in Glue Club is being like, "Is anybody else seeing this?" And that is really valuable. You can do it in Lenny land as well, but just get out there and talk about what's real and what's not. Don't just stay in a sad lonely hole.
turns.zh: 好，我说两件事。第一，我从社区和 Glue Club 得到了很多智慧，也得到很多对这类对话的支持。我觉得如果你是一位领导者，听着这期节目感到孤独、有点得不到支持，那就去找一个社区——不管是 Glue Club 还是别的——在那里你可以谈论这些。因为我确实认为，互相依靠去了解什么是真实的、什么不是，什么有价值、什么没有——我们在 Glue Club 做的很多事就是问：“还有别人看到这个吗？”这真的很有价值。你在 Lenny 的地盘也能这么做，但就是走出去，谈论什么是真实的、什么不是。不要只是待在一个悲伤孤独的洞里。

turns.en: But the second thing I wanted to say, Lenny, is thank you for making space for this. I think it's important. There's so much space right now for the "what should I do" and "what skills should I get" and "what course should I take" and "what tool should I try next, who's hot today." But we aren't talking enough about the human side of this and what it feels like to be going through this for everyone. And so I'm grateful that you reached out and we talked about making space to talk about this, because I think hopefully people will leave feeling a little more sane and like, "Oh, everybody else is feeling a little crazy right now, too." And there's lots of people out there grieving, and that's okay. That's normal. So, thank you, Lenny.
turns.zh: 但我想说的第二件事，Lenny，是谢谢你为这件事留出空间。我觉得这很重要。现在有太多空间留给“我该做什么”“我该学什么技能”“我该上什么课”“我下一个该试什么工具、今天谁最火”。但我们没有足够地谈论这件事人性的一面，以及每个人经历这一切时的感受。所以我很感激你主动联系我，我们谈到要留出空间来聊这个，因为我想，希望人们离开时会觉得更清醒一点，觉得“哦，原来其他人现在也有点疯”。外面有很多人在悲伤，这没关系。这很正常。所以，谢谢你，Lenny。

turns.en: Thank you, Molly. I think of these—I have a term for these sorts of episodes. I call them Trojan horse episodes, where people come for all this tactical concrete stuff: "I need to know how do I use AI in this way? How do I become a better PM?" And then there's these like—
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Molly。我觉得这类节目——我对这类节目有个说法。我叫它们特洛伊木马节目，人们冲着这些战术性的具体内容来：“我需要知道怎么这样用 AI？我怎么成为更好的产品经理？”然后就有这些——

turns.en: You get therapy.
turns.zh: 你得到了心理治疗。

turns.en: Important episodes that slip right in. Yeah, exactly. You're like, "Oh, okay. I didn't know I needed that, but that was very helpful."
turns.zh: 重要的节目就这么溜进来了。是的，没错。你会说：“哦，好吧。我不知道我需要这个，但那真的很有帮助。”

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So, well, welcome to the Trojan horse smuggling in.
turns.zh: 那么，欢迎特洛伊木马偷偷溜进来。

turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。

turns.en: Very timely with the Odyssey these days, huh?
turns.zh: 最近跟《奥德赛》很应景，是吧？

turns.en: Yeah, dude.
turns.zh: 是啊，老兄。

turns.en: All right, Molly. Well, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 好了，Molly。非常感谢你来。

turns.en: Yeah. Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的。谢谢你邀请我，Lenny。

turns.en: Bye, everyone.
turns.zh: 大家再见。

turns.en: Bye, everybody.
turns.zh: 大家再见。

consensus.en: Change is scary and hard, but leaning into it beats holding on.
consensus.zh: 变化令人恐惧且艰难，但主动拥抱它胜过死守不放。

consensus.en: The future belongs to learners, not knowers; standing still means falling behind.
consensus.zh: 未来属于学习者而非已知者；原地不动就意味着落后。

consensus.en: Treat AI as a junior intern needing context, coaching, and iteration.
consensus.zh: 把 AI 当作需要上下文、指导和反复迭代的初级实习生。

consensus.en: Grief over lost work is real; leaders must normalize these emotions.
consensus.zh: 对失去工作的悲伤是真实的；领导者必须让这些情绪正常化。

consensus.en: Managers are the strongest lever for workplace happiness; management matters more now.
consensus.zh: 管理者是职场幸福感最强的杠杆；如今管理更加重要。

consensus.en: Humans must guide toward the world we want, not just the optimal AI output.
consensus.zh: 人类必须引导走向我们想要的世界，而非仅仅追求 AI 的最优输出。

contrarian.en: Some Legos should never be given away; not all work should be outsourced to AI.
contrarian.zh: 有些乐高永远不该送人；并非所有工作都该外包给 AI。

contrarian.en: AI-branded layoffs are mostly badly run companies, not genuine AI job replacement.
contrarian.zh: 打着 AI 旗号的裁员多半是经营不善的公司，而非 AI 真正取代了工作。

contrarian.en: Delegating to AI isn't giving away Legos; you still own the oversight burden.
contrarian.zh: 把任务交给 AI 不等于送出乐高；你仍然背负着监督的重担。

contrarian.en: We're in a slow takeoff, not a fast one; there's time to adapt.
contrarian.zh: 我们处于慢速起飞而非快速起飞；仍有时间适应。

contrarian.en: You're not behind; this is inning one, and beginners can catch up fast.
contrarian.zh: 你并没有落后；这才第一局，新手可以快速赶上。

contrarian.en: Cutting management layers is a huge mistake; management matters more, not less.
contrarian.zh: 削减管理层是巨大错误；管理不是更不重要，而是更重要。
